title: Samsung Opens a Quantum Design Lab in Cambridge, Its First Company-Wide Quantum Research Unit
content:
Korea Supply Chain Brief · September 29, 2026

Samsung Electronics has opened a new Quantum Design Lab in Cambridge, Massachusetts and is hiring PhD-level research scientists, its first standalone organization tasked with leading quantum computing research across the entire company rather than one business unit. Here is what the new lab does and why it marks a shift from Samsung's earlier, more indirect approach to quantum technology.

CompanyRoleEvidence
Samsung Electronics
KRX: 005930		Opened a new Quantum Design Lab in Cambridge, MA, hiring quantum computing researchersReported (industry trade press, Sep 29, 2026)

What was reported

  • Location: a leased building in Cambridge, Massachusetts, near Harvard and MIT, operated through Samsung Semiconductor Inc. (SSI), Samsung's U.S. semiconductor subsidiary.
  • Hiring: SSI is recruiting Research Scientists for the lab, requiring a PhD in a quantum-computing-related field, with applications open through December 1.
  • Scope: the lab is described as leading quantum computing research across Samsung Electronics as a whole, not tied to a single business unit, covering quantum error correction (QEC), quantum architecture, benchmarking, and quantum algorithms — foundational theory and system design rather than a specific product.
  • Formed: the report says the lab was newly set up in the second half of this year.

Why this is a shift from Samsung's earlier approach

The report frames this as a departure from Samsung's past pattern of engaging with quantum computing mainly through equity investments in external startups or indirect support, toward direct in-house research. The strategy described is to have Samsung's headquarters directly lead core theoretical work and system architecture design, aiming to internalize next-generation quantum source technology rather than rely on outside partners for it.

Samsung's quantum research had previously run mainly through its Samsung Advanced Institute of Technology (SAIT), the group's advanced R&D organization, but the report says that work narrowed as semiconductor priorities took precedence, before a recent group-level push to restore and expand quantum investment. In January, Samsung brought in Park Hong-geun — a former Harvard chemistry and physics chair professor — to head SAIT; the report quotes him discussing preemptive investment across multiple quantum modalities and algorithms, aiming to move beyond a "fast follower" position.

Why Cambridge specifically

The report describes the Cambridge/Boston area as home to the world's largest quantum ecosystem, anchored by Harvard and MIT along with a dense cluster of quantum startups. Samsung's stated plan is to use that local network to directly recruit global research talent and accelerate research through open academic partnerships with the universities there.

Related hardware and near-term technology moves

  • Patent: Samsung has registered a patent in Korea and the U.S. for increasing the integration density of superconducting qubits, using 3D placement of memory elements to scale up computation while reducing external noise interference — described as an attempt to apply Samsung's semiconductor stacking know-how to quantum chips.
  • Manufacturing application: Samsung's semiconductor research lab and Samsung SDS are separately pursuing a project applying quantum computing algorithms to resolve computational bottlenecks in optical proximity correction (OPC) simulation for sub-2nm angstrom-class process nodes.
  • Security: Samsung has already begun mass-producing a hardware post-quantum cryptography (PQC) security chip, which won a Best Innovation Award at CES 2026.

What is not disclosed

  • Headcount targets, budget, or a research timeline for the Quantum Design Lab.
  • Named university or startup partners in the Cambridge ecosystem.
  • A commercialization roadmap connecting this research organization to any specific future product.

A Samsung Electronics representative is quoted confirming the lab is newly established and led by an executive at the vice-president level, but said specific organizational structure and research plans could not be disclosed.

Quick FAQ

What did Samsung just announce?
Nothing formally announced; a new Quantum Design Lab in Cambridge, Massachusetts was reported based on a hiring posting from Samsung Semiconductor Inc., its U.S. subsidiary.

Is this lab tied to a specific Samsung product?
No. It is described as covering foundational quantum computing research — error correction, architecture, algorithms — across the whole company, not a single business unit or product line.

How is this different from Samsung's past quantum computing activity?
Samsung had previously engaged with quantum computing mainly through investments in external startups; this is Samsung directly running in-house foundational research for the first time in a dedicated, company-wide organization.
